Phases of rare $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decays are sensitive to CP-violating effects and are therefore an important benchmark for the scientific validity of $B$-factory experiments. To fully exploit these capabilities, it is crucial to assess the effective lifetime of this decay, which can be achieved through studies of same-side and opposite-side processes by which the neutral $B$ meson is produced. This report outlines methods for determining the effective lifetime in same-side and opposite-side processes and presents theoretical predictions for both cases. Numerical calculations indicate that the average lifetime of $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ can be measured with a high degree of precision, ranging from 0.38 to 3.4 ps, depending on the specific transition. This analysis also explores strategies for optimizing the measurement of the $B^0_s\rightarrow \gamma K^+K^-$ decay time or rare $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decays at hadron colliders.

This research paper focuses on the second-order stability analysis of a discrete control issue with delays in the state equation and a Carath\'eodory solution, using a weak formulation. Key advancements are made in establishing the existence and characterization of a compact family of invariant sets, as well as in proving the asymptotic stability of the equilibrium solution for a variety of state delay structures.

Our comprehensive study of the Pierre Auger Observatory's extensive air showers induced by cosmic rays reveals a complex anisotropic pattern when observed at the highest energies, specifically above 4 EeV. By employing a sophisticated method to account for the detector's sensitivity and variations in atmospheric conditions, we identified significant anisotropies in the arrival directions of these cosmic rays. We observed a strong signal of approximately 3.2 sigma relative intensity along the Galactic center and detected two relatively faint but distinct directional signals of around 3.4 sigma each, located in the constellations of Telescopium and Piscis-Cauda at a significance of approximately 5.5 degrees. Furthermore, we found that these anisotropies persist even after conducting a comprehensive search for anisotropies on smaller angular scales, which is crucial for distinguishing genuine celestial phenomena from directional signals resulting from the Earth's rotation and the distribution of air showers within the detector. Given the uniform response of the detector to the cosmic rays, we can rule out any anisotropies in the energy spectrum or composition, which could give rise to anisotropies during the propagation of high-energy particles through the cosmos.
This paper proves that any finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra over a field characterized by not being simultaneously commutative and power-commutative has a solvability index of two.

The newly developed THESIS method, which analyzes particle distributions within the momentum space to identify flow characteristics, has been applied to lead-lead collisions at the Large Hadron Collider's nominal energy. Investigating the orientation of flow in these collisions, researchers have found that the angular distribution of particles can be fitted with a combination of four harmonic vibrations. Furthermore, examinations of particle distributions within the momentum space have revealed that the collisions' properties can be reproduced using an interacting quantum field model. By correlating particles and anti-particles, researchers have confirmed the same flow direction and intensity in both cases, thereby validating the conservation of charge symmetry in the collisions.

Tables with functional relationships and null values can be challenging to integrate, especially when there are inconsistencies between them. In this project, we are developing techniques to accommodate these discrepancies and identify consistent facts. A key aspect is managing the complexity of the data by providing options for how the data is structured, including the choice of background tables and whether to use union, intersection, or difference operations. Additionally, we are exploring ways to make the data more versatile by incorporating a module system that allows for the integration of nested queries and user-defined functions. This approach is part of a broader project aimed at creating a flexible and efficient data integration framework that can handle diverse data sources and various data relationships.

The study examines time-series data from count distributions to extend the fundamental principles of the ARIMA model. We propose a novel type of model, TV-PARX, which encompasses models from non-Zero-mean ARIMA through negative binomial ARX. This comprehensive framework allows for flexible parameterization that enables efficient estimation via the method of moments. We also conduct numerical studies to evaluate the performance of our method and apply TV-PARX to real-world datasets.

We introduce Neural Description Fields (NDFs), a novel deep learning object representation
framework that generates textured 3D shapes from verbal descriptions.
NDFs build on the success of graph neural networks and neural collabative filtering,
incorporating SE(3)-equivariant convolutions to ensure rotational invariance.
By leveraging an adversarial training process, NDFs are able to produce 3D shapes
that not only accurately reflect the descriptive input but also are indistinguishable
from real shapes generated randomly.
We showcase the efficacy of NDFs in two tasks: generating 3D shapes from descriptive
input and classifying 3D shapes based on verbal descriptions.
Our results indicate that NDFs outperform existing methods in both scenarios.

Using functional renormalization group, we have the Yang-Lee edge singularity's critical properties near $O(N)$ symmetric points in three dimensions. It is found that the edge singularity's universal parameters are consistent across all $N$ values, revealing a distinctive pattern of deviation from traditional universality classes, particularly evident for $N=2$ and implicitly for $N=10$. Even when slight next-to-leading order corrections are considered, the universal parameters in the vicinity of these symmetric points demonstrate only a minimal variation, suggesting that the Yang-Lee edge criticality could be positioned within a singular point at the intersection of these universality classes.

In statistics and machine learning, it is frequently essential to establish whether a particular minimizer of a random objective function corresponds to a global optimum. To address this, we must compare the distribution of the objective function at this predicted optimum with its actual distribution across all possible solutions. In a recent study, it was demonstrated that around an ideal transition point, the distribution of the objective function in the most probable state differs from the mean of all possible solutions by at most a constant factor. Here, we enhance this result by showing that the distribution of the objective function in the most probable state surrounds the mean of all possible solutions at a rate that decreases exponentially with the square of the distance from the ideal transition point. This indicates that around the ideal transition point, the predicted optimum is nearly globally optimal. To achieve this, we apply a variant of the Sudakov-Fernique anti-concentration inequality and a new variant of the Talagrand-Petrec method.

While observing the cosmos, astronomical data can be affected by various disturbances in the data, especially those resulting from aerosol accumulation within the telescope's system. This kind of issue can be mitigated from general techniques for data analysis but might conceal a more significant issue - a systematic error affecting photographic magnitude measurements. We aim to address this limitation by developing a new method for calculating the amount of aerosol based on photographic magnitude measurements in the context of planetary science. This technique involves a linear model where the quantity of aerosol represents the main subject of analysis, and we've developed a Bayesian approach to estimate this quantity. Furthermore, we applied this method to data from the Cassini mission and discovered that the quantity of aerosol varied over time, which is a significant finding in its own right. This study is relevant to a broad range of current and future planetary science missions that rely on imaging techniques for observing the surroundings of other planets and utilize stellar targets for calibrating data.

Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using images has gained significant interest. Researchers distinguish between two primary approaches: regression-based methods, which directly predict the object's 6D pose by feeding a single image into the network, and clustering-based methods, which utilize a pre-trained network to map an input image to a low-dimensional feature space and determine the object's pose based on its projected 2D coordinates on an arbitrary plane. Despite both categories of methods being developed independently, there is potential for cross-fertilization of ideas. Building upon the clustering-based method called DeepHMap, we introduce an end-to-end framework called DeepHMap++ that combines both categories of methods by employing a novel, hybrid architecture. DeepHMap++ leverages a dual-pipeline design where, in addition to the clustering-based pipeline, we integrate a regression-based pipeline into the network. By connecting the two pipelines, we establish a shared feature set that enables the network to learn a unified, compact representation of the object's features. To further enhance the performance of our proposed framework, we introduce two novel loss functions called the learned-2D loss and the learned-clustering loss, which facilitate the network in directly extracting a 6D pose from an image. Evaluating our proposed framework on three public datasets affirms its superiority over both the regression-based and clustering-based single-pipeline models.

We present GGLasso, a Python-based library for Generalized Graphical Lasso estimation
on multi-view data with positive and zero entries. This development aims to address
the limitation of existing methods in modeling multi-view data with a high number of
features and non-isolated variables. Existing algorithms require a pre-step where
each view is normalized to ensure identical variance, which can result in the loss
of meaningful relationships between views. Our approach, embedded in the GGLasso package,
employs an alternative formulation to directly apply the Graphical Lasso on each view
individually while maintaining the relationship between views. This is demonstrated on
simulated and real-world data, including gene expression data from The Cancer Genome
Atlas (TCGA), showing improved estimation compared to existing multi-view Graphical Lasso
methods.

Numerous applications in chemistry and physics rely on molecular dynamics simulations, which provide valuable configurations for subsequent calculations. Yet, simultaneously performing these calculations and executing dynamics simulations simultaneously is often challenging due to differing time scales, especially when electron and nuclear motions are in play. To tackle this issue, various methods sample configuration spaces via dynamics simulations, taking advantage of the natural exploration brought about through thermostatted Langevin dynamics. In the course of studying critical phenomena with ring polymers, we developed a method that leverages these dynamics simulations to generate configurations while accurately describing local density fluctuations. Our method proves to be both efficient and precise, surpassing conventional Metropolis algorithms in terms of computational requirements while maintaining comparable precision. By utilizing these dynamics simulations in combination with a local topological rule, we obtained reliable estimates for the free energy of ring polymer nanoconstrictions. Our approach is universally applicable to a broad range of problems, from biological to solid state, and even materials science, by extending the validity of Langevin dynamics to heavy atoms and providing an accurate means of sampling high-energy states.

Understanding the structure of complex networks is a key aspect that affects how information spreads, how diseases transmit, and how influential an individual will be. As a result, researchers constantly seek new methods to analyze and assess the significance of network nodes. In multilayer networks, defined by distinct time periods or types of information, this task is even more critical due to the dynamic nature of relationships and the need to consider time-dependent and community-based asset reliance. To address this challenge, research has focused on interpreting the meaning of eigenvector centrality across static networks. However, there is limited knowledge about how to interpret the significance of eigenvectors within static networks and especially within multilayer networks. Our study provides a novel framework for interpreting the significance of eigenvectors within static networks and multilayer networks. We discovered that the promotion of eigenvector centrality at individual nodes is directly tied to their asset reliance and community attachment. Furthermore, we found that the promotion of eigenvector centrality can be understood through the analysis of multilayer networks' layered structure. Our research also involves applying this new framework to investigate the dynamics of asset reliance and community attachment across different network layers. We found that asset reliance and community attachment tend to change gradually over time, although the rate of change varies depending on the network layer. Our study provides a starting point for further research on the subject, such as examining the statistical properties of eigenvector centrality or investigating the implications of our findings for real-world applications

Recently, we established the existence and uniqueness of solutions to the Dirac equation in Riemannian spacetimes that possess a specific symmetry and are nearly flat. Within a specific Riemannian spacetime framework, defined by the Riemannian metric being closely related to a flat Minkowski metric, we demonstrated that the only solutions to the Dirac equation are those that can be determined from the operator algebra acting on a one-dimensional complex space. Building on this foundation, we derived an explicit formula for solutions to the Dirac equation within a specific Riemannian spacetime framework, effectively reinterpreting a well-known result from special relativity in this context.

This study delves into the mechanics of sphere seals occurring on the surface of a rotating liquid, specifically within the moderate Reynolds number range (1000-10000). The research focuses on the mechanical aspects of these seals at the point of contact, particularly where the liquid surface meets the sphere's lower surface. The primary contact region is divided into two sub-regions: a central area near the axis of rotation where the liquid moves in the same direction as the sphere, and a surrounding area where the liquid moves opposite to the sphere's direction. The research reveals that an annular region around the axis of rotation experiences reduced pressure compared to the surrounding liquid pressure. Furthermore, the size of this reduced pressure area is found to be directly proportional to the viscosity of the liquid. The research also finds that the seals created on the sphere's surface are not uniform and vary in depth across different sub-regions. The depth of these seals is found to be influenced by the viscosity of the liquid, with the deepest seals observed near the axis of rotation. The research indicates that the relationship between the depth of these seals and the distance from the axis of rotation follows a parabolic pattern. The relationship between the sphere's speed and the depth of these seals is found to be directly proportional, while the relationship between the sphere's speed and the size of the reduced pressure area is found to be proportional to the square of the sphere's speed. A well-known hypothesis posits that quantum gravity at very high energies exhibits maximal symmetry to prevent paradoxes. While this isn't a strict requirement, it does lead to interesting consequences when combined with the concept of universal symmetry breaking. In the framework of effective field theories, even a generic effective action in Type IIB supergravity contains highly symmetric components that can be identified through an extended theta-term at the three-form field transformation. A systematic exploration of these components can uncover the fundamental operators of which the effective action is composed. By applying this method to a general effective action in Type IIB supergravity, we identify a universal, universal symmetry-breaking sector hidden within the extended theta-terms, which arises from a combination of the axion sector, E$_3$ gauge field triangulation, and Riemann surface instantons. This discovery fills in the missing pieces of the effective action's landscape and offers a deeper comprehension of the underlying principles of universal symmetry breaking.

Our calculations using first-principles methods reveal that cubanite exhibits unusual orbital properties, with a specific energy gap affecting some of its iron ions' behavior. This phenomenon is unusually complex due to cubanite's unique crystal structure, which allows for multiple arrangements of its electrons. By simulating the actual structure of the material, we were able to identify areas of high electron density that influence the orbital behavior and suggested the existence of an unusual type of bond called van der Waals bonding between certain cubanite molecules.

A burgeoning field in quantum physics, known as discrete or driven systems physics, is influencing the study of complex phenomena in many areas. Researchers have successfully achieved Rabi oscillations between different quantum states using various methods and in different systems. However, achieving large-amplitude Rabi oscillations between two distinct quantum states under steady-state conditions poses a significant challenge. A team of scientists recently discovered a way to achieve these large-amplitude Rabi oscillations between two distinct quantum states within a semiconductor quantum dot system that are driven by light. They demonstrated that even when the external light is strong, even if it's over a thousand times more powerful than the quantum system it's interacting with, it's possible to prevent the oscillations from breaking down by utilizing two drive lights that are slightly different in frequency. This remarkable finding also enables the development of extremely sensitive detectors that can accurately identify the quantum state of a system even when the system itself is vast, not a tiny particle.

Our investigation focuses on a 2D wallpaper lattice that belongs to a non-symmorphic group. This lattice stands out due to its unique 2D microrystal structure composed of hexagonally arranged hexagons, incorporating six-fold rotation symmetry within each individual hexagon. This structure can be physically realized through coupling of hexagonally shaped nitrogen atoms to carbon nanocuboids in a BN crystal. The resulting hybrid lattice exhibits an intriguing capacity to adjust its geometric configuration, thereby tunably altering the properties of its Dirac cones. By adjusting the size of the hexagons relative to each other, we discovered the opportunity to move the location of these cones along the k-space, a feature that can be particularly useful for guiding the behavior of fermionic particles in this system. Furthermore, we observed the potential for all-electronic control over mass terms and curvature in a 2D lattice, a breakthrough that can be achieved simply by attaching different atoms to the cuboids. Notably, this phenomenon results in a novel type of topological phase that can be induced through chemical modification alone.

Quantum states known as single-photon facilitated coherent states (SPFCS) possess unique properties that make them exceptionally robust against photon loss. These states are characterized by a minimal number of photons, ensuring effective utilization of the available photon resource. SPFCS also exhibit simplified dynamics in comparison to standard coherent states, with an accelerated transition between state components following the loss of a specific photon number. In the scenario of continuous variables, quantum states facilitating quantum-optical catalysis can serve as catalysts, maintaining the stability of coherent states for an extended period. We examine SPFCS generated through quantum-optical catalysis, investigating various state preparation methods and associated challenges. Notably, we evaluate the efficiency of a specific quantum-optical catalysis setup, situated within a lossy cavity, utilizing a laser as the driving source. Additionally, we investigate different catalysis configurations, including one utilizing a nonlinear crystal, and provide guidelines for optimizing the catalysis effectiveness while minimizing quantum noise. Theoretical insights into these systems are supported by numerical simulations, offering a foundation for experimental verification.

In General Relativity using the Newman-Penrose formalism, the use of bivectors plays a key role in identifying the electromagnetic field within the Weyl tensor. This review focuses on explaining the fundamental concepts of bivectors, demonstrates their utility in the Newman-Penrose formalism, and specifically delves into the decomposition of the Weyl tensor through the Edwards-Batsanov method.

In 2019, the concept of Polymers was introduced as a new theoretical framework 
integrating the ideas behind Implicit Programs and Resource Separation, offering 
a novel perspective on program safety verification. Building on this foundation, 
we aim to expand the capabilities of Polymers by developing a method for 
deducting polymers based on a comprehensive analysis of program behavior, 
enabling the detection of unnecessary restrictions in program safety proofs. 
This technique, which we call Contextual Deduction, employs a straightforward 
statistical technique to identify polymers that can be safely removed from a 
program, leaving its behavioral consequences unchanged. To support and illustrate 
the effectiveness of Contextual Deduction, we present an experimental study 
conducting deductions on ten real-world programs written in a higher-order 
functional programming language, including programs containing polymers that can 
be safely eliminated, demonstrating that our technique is capable of 
accurately identifying these removable polymers.

We introduce a novel image segmentation technique called Dilated Dense Focus Unet (DDAUnet) for effectively identifying multiple classes within a single image. This approach builds on the dense connection Unet (DCUnet) model and the patch-based method. By dividing the image into distinct regions, we employ both local and global information to define boundaries and identify neoplastic content. This strategy simplifies classification and reduces Computed Tomography (CT) image noise effects. To demonstrate the potential of DDAUnet, we used it to segment esophageal tumors from CT scans. With several improvements, the algorithm outperforms comparable state-of-the-art methods and provides a strong foundation for further research, such as using DDAUnet for multi-task esophageal tumor analysis.

Multilingual individuals possess a high level of linguistic proficiency in two or more languages, enabling effective written and oral communication across those languages. These individuals face unique challenges such as code-switching, diminished monolingual knowledge, and varying degrees of knowledge in each language. Furthermore, they encounter distinct obstacles like linguistic interference, knowledge dispersion, and differing language usage in written and oral communication. These obstacles affect not only their daily interactions but also various language-related tasks like part-of-speech tagging, sentiment analysis, and machine translation. In response, researchers are exploring new theories and models, such as multilingual modular processing, transfer learning, and neural networks, to better understand the underlying mechanisms and develop more accurate applications like multilingual NLP models, but with limitations. Despite these advancements, numerous questions remain unanswered about the relationships between languages, the nature of code-switching, and the impact on task performance. This study aims to investigate the intricate relationships between languages, explore the complexities of code-switching, and provide a foundation for future research in multilingual NLP.

Describing images automatically has become a sophisticated task with various applications and is now a standard component in visual information systems. Evaluating and further developing this technology rely heavily on empirical evidence obtained through experiments. Although there are established methods for evaluating image description systems, they primarily focus on measuring how well the system's outputs are liked by ordinary people. This study advocates for incorporating more diverse and targeted references into the system's training data to enhance the quality of its descriptions. We tested this idea with a dataset chosen randomly and found that using diverse references during training improves the system's performance. We also explored using reference descriptions that are easily accessible, such as image captions, which can be both a beneficial addition to training data and a source of new training data.

Tantalum oxide in form of Ta$_2$O$_5$ is a highly intriguing material with potential applications in the fields of electronics and photonics. To further understand and analyze its properties, it's essential to establish a foundation by determining its crystal structure in a neutral state. However, Ta$_2$O$_5$ exhibits polymorphism, and its bulk form can be difficult to characterize using conventional methods. We examined five possible Ta$_2$O$_5$ structures, including both octahedrally and tetrahedrally coordinated configurations, to determine the most stable state using both theoretical ab-initio simulations and lattice distortion calculations. Despite initial efforts to isolate a single most stable configuration, variations in lattice parameters and band gaps only minimalized large atomic displacements, indicating the presence of localized vibrations that contribute to the broadening of spectral features and suggest a disordered crystal state. This disordered state is consistent with Monte Carlo simulations performed using the PHONONYSOFT package, which further supports the presence of anharmonic effects in Ta$_2O$_5$.

An analysis of Reddit user interactions across the United States has revealed a large-scale geographic pattern of online information sharing, which we call the Giant Hypernetwork Division (GHD). By applying network division methods, research reveals that users from different GHD regions tend to trust and deceive each other based on their physical proximity. A simulation model incorporating the GHD structure suggests that its complexity can either accelerate or slow the spread of misinformation, depending on various factors such as the size of the network and the degree of user trust. By further examining the effects of pandemic-related travel restrictions on the GHD, researchers found that restrictions in certain areas caused sudden isolation from other regions, leading to increased deception among those users and a greater spread of misinformation. Conversely, in areas with freer movement, there was a significant decrease in deception and the misinformation spread more slowly. These findings are relevant to the ongoing battle against the dissemination of false information online and highlight the significance of considering the complex interplay between geographic distance and online user interactions when developing strategies to contain the spread of misinformation.

Humans employ various auditory descriptions to guide each other through complex tasks, despite having a clear visual understanding of the actions being performed. To enhance collaboration and safety, it is beneficial for robots to accurately interpret these auditory cues, which can signal potential hazards or critical phases of a procedure. To this end, researchers need to understand how humans use sound to describe manipulative activities to robots. This study uses a mixture of features and probabilistic neural networks to train a system that can recognize the acoustic patterns associated with specific tasks, such as the objects being used, the robot's arm being employed, and the activities being performed. It then applies this model to predict relevant information about a task from an audio sample describing that task. When evaluated on a large dataset comprising 12 different instruction scenarios, the system displays superior performance, outperforming a competing method based on deep learning and providing valuable insights into the complex relationships between sound features, spectral properties, and the underlying activities being described.

We translate a key complexity criterion in geometric field theory, known as "triviality," in terms of Euler-Arnold equations and Lie group theory. This analysis reveals that a linear group of constant dimension results in a highly intricate field, whereas a non-linear group like the identity group is considered straightforward. Similarly, we examine the intricacy of fields associated with low-dimensional Lie groups.

Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and systems like Amazon's Alexa, Google Assistant, and Microsoft's BotFramework are being used globally. To understand the performance of these systems, researchers and developers need a standardized method of assessment. Currently, evaluations of conversational systems rely heavily on subjective user feedback, which hinders the effectiveness of rapid iterative development processes. To address this challenge, we present a automated evaluation framework called Converse, which assesses the quality of conversational interactions across various aspects such as usability, effectiveness, and overall satisfaction. Converse conducts an in-depth analysis of dialogue sessions through a set of predefined metrics and provides a comprehensive score for each evaluated system. We demonstrate the utility of Converse by applying it to the evaluation of five different conversational systems and identify areas for improvement. Systems developers can utilize Converse freely for the purpose of developing and testing conversational interfaces.

Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-specific features, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Cooperative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods that focus on selecting a single target domain, MSDCR considers all available domains equally, drawing on a unified feature framework to seamlessly integrate multi-domain information. To address the data sparsity in each domain, MSDCR employs a collaborative and domain-agnostic aspect preference learning approach, incorporating the explicit representation of aspect preferences to facilitate effective knowledge sharing and utilization. To handle feature heterogeneity, MSDCR introduces a multi-task learning-based strategy that enables effective domain adaptation through the formation of a unified feature space. To handle the data sparsity in each domain, MSDCR employs a collaborative and domain-agnostic aspect preference learning approach, incorporating the explicit representation of aspect preferences to facilitate effective knowledge sharing and utilization. To handle the issue of imbalance between dense and sparse domains, MSDCR introduces a sampling-based strategy to rectify this imbalance and extract more valuable information from dense domains. Convex optimization over the efficient set of a conic formulation is a problem with multiple optimal solutions, making standard first-order methods ineffective due to their tendency to get stuck in local minima. To address this issue in organic conic formulations, we develop the Hypatia toolbox, releasing it under the MIT open-source license, and expand it to resolve multi-optimal problems. By applying a variety of techniques, including generating organic formulations and detecting multiple-optimal problems, the Hypatia toolbox provides users with one of the following outcomes: a certificate for uniqueness of the optimal solution, or a pair of conic formulations with unique optimal solutions, whose efficient sets coincide. We further provide a way to resolve multiple-optimal problems by maintaining the efficient set of one formulation and projecting onto it after each iteration, resulting in one of the following outcomes: a certificate for uniqueness of the optimal solution, or the efficient set defining a polyhedron which characterizes the multiple-optimal solutions. We illustrate the effectiveness and applications of the Hypatia toolbox on standard benchmark problems and real-world data from solar parks and wind power.

The accuracy of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is crucial for medical diagnoses, making image quality critical. Since MRI data collection involves many variables, including various scan protocols, equipment, and different locations, ensuring the image quality across these variations can be very time-consuming and expensive. This process is usually carried out by experienced radiologists or MRI operators at individual sites, with a high potential for repeated work across different locations. This paper frames the task of MRI quality assurance as a problem of multi-dimensional generalization, aiming to develop a scalable and efficient method to predict image quality based on low-dimensional features obtained from MRI datasets. This approach enables sites to reduce the number of necessary MR scans while ensuring the image quality meets the required standards, and allows for easy protocol changes without needing new training data. This is achieved through a novel adaptive neighbor expansion technique that enhances performance by utilizing a wide range of input features across different dimensions, and is applied in this project to predict image quality based on a combination of spectral and spatial features. Experimental results using real MRI data demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in predicting image quality across different protocols, equipment, and locations, with a marked improvement over conventional methods.

To understand how privately owned electric vehicles influence the stability of distribution networks, a new method is proposed that analyzes various optimization strategies for EV charging and discharging through artificial agents in a simulated environment. Utilizing multi-agent systems and a Mendel approach, a comprehensive review is presented of how networks are affected when vehicles are managed using different charging techniques such as scheduling, reduction of peaks, and utilization of energy storage. A key finding reveals that optimizing the performance of individual vehicles through agents does not necessarily lead to improved network performance. Conversely, privately owned electric vehicles are found to pose a significant threat to the stability of distribution networks, with potential consequences including increased construction costs for necessary infrastructure and the need for more stringent management policies.

In games like "Meeting" which model real-life social interactions, having multiple moving agents aim to meet at a single point is a common occurrence. Research in computer graphics often focuses on simulations where agents navigate to a meeting point, yet fewer studies exist in the field of artificial intelligence, specifically in incentive-based approaches. This paper presents a new algorithm where multiple non-central agents move to find the meeting point based on local information, and an incentive framework encourages them to move towards the meeting point. This results in all agents converging to the meeting point simultaneously. We apply and test this method on a complex scenario called "Recurring Meeting", a multi-agent scenario where agents move according to simple rules in response to the arrival of other agents, yet share a common goal of meeting at a designated spot. In this scenario, differing incentives affect the interaction dynamics between the agents, leading to various undesirable outcomes like bypassing, collision, or failure to meet. By adjusting these incentives, we can prevent unwanted behaviors and even implement a modular design, enabling easy modification of the interaction dynamics.

This paper examines the structural, electronic, and magnetic properties of GdSn3, CmSn3, and the series GdxCm1-xSn3 ($x = 0.25$, $0.5$, and $0.75$) using a full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method within the generalized gradient approximation+U. We studied the fundamental characteristics of bulk GdSn3, CmSn3, and GdxCm1-xSn3 materials crystallizing in the AuCu3 structure. Our results match previous experimental and theoretical data on the GdSn3 material and indicate that CmSn3 and GdSn3 both adopt a type-A anti-ferromagnetic configuration and display metallic behavior. Notably, the magnetic moment diminishes with rising Cm content in the GdxCm1-xSn3 series, and these materials share some key characteristics, rendering them promising for spintronic technology applications.

The paper discusses the potential emergence of extra baryons and mesons within the framework of a $SU(2)\times SU(2)'$ symmetry, which arises from a $SU(4)_L \times SU(4)_R$ symmetry when applied to four-quark systems. Although the original $SU(4)_L \times SU(4)_R$ symmetry leads to the same mass for all quarks due to mass generation requirements, the $SU(2)\times SU(2)'$ symmetry still offers valuable insights by providing a relationship between the masses of different particles. Consequently, the paper derives a classification of extra baryons and mesons based on this symmetry, resulting in mass formulas for various combinations of quarks. Notably, these formulas can be tested and refined using physical particle masses, thereby offering a direct path to understanding the underlying dynamics that determine quark masses.

The Coxeter groups, which include the finite and extended crystallographic groups, serve as a natural extension of the finite automorphism groups that act on a Euclidean space through isometries. These groups, however, do not automatically guarantee a favorable geometric understanding, as many of their properties are derived from the inherent structure of the Coxeter system rather than direct implications of the group's properties. In fact, the absence of specific combinatorial characteristics, such as root systems, complicates the application of standard analytical techniques. This study aims to fill this gap by developing a general framework for translating the geometric properties defined by a set of generators and corresponding relations into the language of roots and mirrors, allowing the application of established theoretical tools to the finite Coxeter groups, thereby extending previous works by the authors for finite and half-linear groups to all B-type Coxeter groups.

A interesting effect of gravitational lensing, particularly strong lensing, is the variation in the brightness of gravitational objects, where multiple images of a single event are observed with different luminosities.  Research has shown that even weak lensing can influence the characteristics of observable events in the cosmos.  One notable phenomenon that can be affected by weak lensing is the expansion history of the universe as inferred from Type Ia Supernovae data.  Although weak lensing can cause a scatter in SN Ia luminosities, its overall impact on the measurement of the cosmic expansion rate should be minimal.  However, by categorizing SN Ia data based on their luminosity, it may be possible to detect a signal from weak lensing, which could provide a more precise estimate of the density of matter in the universe.
